title: Design exercise: notifications
summary: A classic design exercise: a shared notification service for push, email and SMS with preferences, quiet hours, provider failover and no duplicates. The reference answer uses an idempotency key per (event, user, channel), one durable queue per channel and priority class, adapters behind circuit breakers with a secondary provider, collapse identifiers at the provider, and a delivery status store; the design-doc frame follows the outline's worked example.

exercise.prompt: Design a notification service that several product teams use to send push, email and SMS to users. A user must see each event once, on the channels they allow and not during their quiet hours; a provider outage must not stop delivery; the sending team must be able to ask what happened to a notification.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: An API for internal teams to send a notification for an event to a user on one or more channels; per-user preferences and quiet hours; templates per team.
Delivery status by notification id; provider failover; retries without duplicates.
20 million users; 50 million notifications per day.
70 percent push, 25 percent email, 5 percent SMS.
Peak 10 times the daily average; five sending teams today, more later.
derive the per-second rates per channel and the queue sizes yourself
Push handed to the provider within 5 s at p95; email within 60 s; SMS within 30 s; provider failover within 60 s of detection.
At-least-once delivery to the provider with deduplication so a user sees one message per event; 99.9 percent availability of the send API.
Marketing campaigns and audience selection, an in-app inbox, analytics beyond delivery status, exactly-once delivery across providers (not possible end to end).

clarifying_questions.a: The sending team proposes channels per event type; the user's preferences and quiet hours filter them; the service never adds a channel the team did not ask for.

clarifying_questions.q: What is the duplicate we must prevent?
clarifying_questions.a: The same event sent twice by a retrying caller, and the same queued notification processed twice by a retrying consumer. The same event sent with two different event ids by the caller is not caught, and the API contract says so.
Push and SMS are held until the window ends (or dropped if the event expires); email is sent, since it does not wake anyone (assumption; a product decision the doc must state).
Two: transactional (security codes, receipts) which ignores quiet hours and rate limits, and informational which honours both.

clarifying_questions.q: How long is delivery status kept?
clarifying_questions.a: 90 days (assumption), queryable by notification id and by user.
Phone numbers and device tokens only inside the adapter boundary and the status store, encrypted at rest; teams send user ids, never addresses.

blocks.text: One API in front of a preference lookup, one durable queue per channel and priority class (six queues) with competing consumers, provider adapters behind circuit breakers with a secondary provider each, a delivery status store written from provider callbacks, and a dead-letter queue with an operator view. The channel queues are separate because the channels have different latency targets and different providers; a shared queue would let an SMS backlog delay push. Fan-out of one event to several channels happens at the API, the way a publish-subscribe topic fans one message out to several queues.

blocks.legend: The accept half of the architecture, the same boxes as the neutral diagram's left side, one AWS service each: the API is an ECS on Fargate service behind an internal load balancer, the preference lookup is a Valkey cache over a DynamoDB table, the delivery status is a DynamoDB table that also holds the idempotency key items (with a TTL), and the six channel queues are SQS standard queues. The load balancer is the entry the neutral diagram leaves implicit; the held table and the release poller (a function that EventBridge Scheduler invokes on a one-minute schedule s10) carry the quiet-hours hold of the neutral design. Each arrow says how the call is made: HTTPS and HTTP inside the VPC, named SDK calls over the gateway endpoint s11 and the SQS interface endpoint s12, cache reads and writes. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has been answered. The VPC frame is one VPC in one Region across three Availability Zones. Inside the quiet hours the record starts in state held, one of the states of the neutral data model, and a retry skips it. The held table is keyed by user and channel, sorted by release time, with a sparse index by release minute plus a shard number so that a morning's releases do not pile onto one key range; the index costs extra write units s30 and the shard number is write sharding s67. The preferences box also holds the templates (key team and template, one item per version with an active-version marker and a kill switch), the cache holds the templates too, and the API serves the three calls besides a send: GET a status (a GetItem, or a Query of the index by user), PUT preferences (a PutItem and a DEL of the cache entry) and POST a template (a conditional PutItem of the next version). The notifications table has two indexes, by user and by provider message id, each projecting the keys only; every entry written to an index costs a further write unit s30.

blocks.text: The key is read first because a known key is the cheap case, and the transaction then writes the key item and the records together: either all of them exist or none, so a retry never finds a key without its records. A key item is deleted by DynamoDB some time after its day is over, and the deletion may lag by days, so the check compares the timestamp itself. The channels inside the quiet hours are decided before the transaction, so their records start in state held, one of the states of the neutral data model, and the held items are written in the same transaction; a retry skips them. Transactional notifications skip the quiet-hours and limit checks, as the priority class says. A known key is answered from the records themselves: the API reads their states, enqueues the ones still queued and skips the held ones. The templates are read through the cache and rendered before the transaction; a template whose kill switch is set is refused.

blocks.caption: The channel queues: SQS standard, SQS FIFO, SNS in front of SQS, or a stream.

rows.option: Amazon SQS standard queues, one per channel and priority class
rows.pick_when: work is handed to one consumer group, at-least-once delivery is fine because the work is idempotent, each message needs its own retry and dead-letter handling, and consumers scale on the age of the queue
rows.avoid_when: several independent consumers each need every event, or the order of messages matters
rows.example: For this design: chosen, six queues, so an SMS backlog never delays push. The adapters make a redelivery harmless by checking the record first, and the age of the oldest message is both the alarm and the scaling signal.

rows.pick_when: strict order within a group matters and a short window of deduplication is a help
rows.avoid_when: the deduplication needed is longer than 5 minutes, or no order is needed
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. FIFO deduplicates sends only within 5 minutes, while the idempotency key lives for 24 hours, so the key table still does the real work, and nothing here needs an order across notifications.

rows.option: Amazon SNS in front of one SQS queue per consumer
rows.pick_when: one publish should reach several consumers, each with its own queue, retries and dead-letter queue, and subscription filters can route by attribute
rows.avoid_when: the producer already knows the one queue each message belongs to, so the topic is an extra hop and an extra publish
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The API holds one record per channel and sends each to its queue, which the neutral design calls fan-out at the API; a topic returns the day a second system wants every notification.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon MSK
rows.pick_when: consumers need per-key order, replay of retained history, or many readers of the same stream
rows.avoid_when: each message is an independent unit of work with its own retries and dead letter
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A notification is a unit of work, not a record in a log, and a stream cannot retry or park one message without holding the shard behind it.

blocks.caption: The stores: DynamoDB or Aurora and RDS, and a cache for the preferences.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB on-demand: status, idempotency keys, preferences, held items, tokens and addresses
rows.pick_when: every access is by one key or one index, retention can be enforced by a TTL, writes are bursty, and nobody wants to plan capacity
rows.avoid_when: teams need ad hoc queries and joins across notifications, templates and users
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the tables. The status is read by notification id and by user, the preferences by user and the keys by event, user and channel; the 90-day retention and the 24-hour key are TTL attributes, so the stores hold the data for at least that long and delete it later, not on the second. The notifications table alone comes to about $9,020 a month.

rows.option: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL or Amazon RDS
rows.pick_when: the product needs joins and ad hoc reporting across notifications, or the team's relational tooling is the asset to keep
rows.avoid_when: the access pattern is a handful of key lookups, so always-on instances idle for a shape a key-value table serves
rows.example: For this design: the fit if reporting becomes a requirement; not chosen now, because analytics beyond delivery status is a non-goal and the status store is a lookup by id with an index by user.

rows.option: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey in front of the preferences, with the per-user counters
rows.pick_when: values are small and read on every request, and the same cluster needs atomic counters with an expiry for token buckets
rows.avoid_when: the working set is small enough for the table alone and nobody wants one more cluster
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The 5,800 preference reads a second at the peak are a cache job, and the per-user and per-team limits are counters that need an atomic increment with a window; two small nodes with a replica cost about $260 a month.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the preferences
rows.pick_when: the cache is a read-through in front of reads by key, and writes can go through the cluster so entries refresh on write
rows.avoid_when: the same cache must also hold counters, which are not table items
rows.example: For this design: a close second for the preferences alone: it would refresh an entry when the preference is updated, which is the invalidation the neutral design wants. Not chosen because the token buckets would still need a second cache.

blocks.caption: Reaching the providers: from the adapters, or through Amazon SNS mobile push.

rows.option: The adapters call the providers directly: APNs and FCM over HTTP/2, Amazon SES, AWS End User Messaging SMS
rows.pick_when: one component should own each provider's headers, tokens, retries and failover, and see the outcome of every attempt
rows.avoid_when: nobody wants to manage device tokens or provider connections
rows.example: For this design: chosen. This is the neutral adapter boundary. APNs takes a collapse identifier and an expiry on each request, which is the duplicate control the design relies on, and a secondary email or SMS provider sits behind the same adapter.

rows.pick_when: the team wants platform endpoints and device-token handling as a managed service and accepts a price per push
rows.avoid_when: the adapter must keep control of each request's headers and of its own failover
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for push. It would be a provider behind the adapter at $0.50 per million pushes, about $525 a month for a hop the adapter already makes, and the circuit breaker and the secondary provider stay the adapter's job either way.

blocks.caption: Holding for the quiet hours: a held table and a poller, EventBridge Scheduler, or an SQS delay.

rows.option: A held table in DynamoDB and a poller on a one-minute schedule
rows.pick_when: many notifications are released in time slots, each user's held set must be capped and collapsed, and the release moment is local time
rows.avoid_when: a few exact-time actions are wanted
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The held table is keyed by user and channel and sorted by release time, so the cap per user, newest winning, is one Query and one delete on that partition; a sparse index by release minute with a shard number lists what is due, and one function every minute queries it, drops what is past its expiry and sends the rest to the channel queues.

rows.option: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, one schedule per held notification
rows.pick_when: a modest number of exact-time actions, each with its own target and retry policy
rows.avoid_when: millions of schedules a day would be created, updated by the collapse and deleted
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Every collapse of a held set would rewrite a schedule, and the volume is a database's, not a scheduler's; the scheduler is used once, for the one-minute poll.

rows.pick_when: a delay of a few minutes between two steps
rows.avoid_when: the delay is hours, because the maximum is 15 minutes
rows.example: For this design: ruled out. Quiet hours last hours, and a message cannot be made invisible for longer than 15 minutes.

blocks.caption: The compute: Fargate, Lambda or EKS.

rows.pick_when: steady, container-shaped services that hold connections and run for as long as there is work, with no cluster to patch
rows.avoid_when: the load is bursty and mostly idle, or the platform team runs Kubernetes for everything else
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the API and the channel adapters, on Arm tasks across three Availability Zones. The API is sized for the peak at about $520 a month, a near tie with a function at about $600 (30 ms at 512 MB, assumption); the adapters keep their provider connections open between messages and scale on queue age.

rows.pick_when: event-shaped work: short, stateless, one trigger, and idle between events
rows.avoid_when: the load is steady and high, or the handler must keep connections open
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the release poller and the callback handler, which wake on a schedule or on an event and sleep otherwise. The API is the close alternative, a near tie on cost, and would move to functions if its traffic became spiky and small.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and needs its ecosystem or portability across clouds
rows.avoid_when: a few services and no Kubernetes estate; the cluster fee and the upgrade cadence buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs the Kubernetes API, and a cluster brings three major releases a year to track for two services.

blocks.caption: The front door for the sending teams: an internal load balancer, or API Gateway.

rows.pick_when: the callers are inside the VPC or its connected networks, and the service enforces its own per-team limits
rows.avoid_when: the platform wants per-client keys, quotas and throttling from a managed layer
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The per-team limits count notifications and the SMS they cause, which the service's own counters do beside the per-user limits; the load balancer costs about $41 a month.

rows.option: Amazon API Gateway REST API with a usage plan per team
rows.pick_when: clients are identified by API keys and each needs its own rate, burst and quota
rows.avoid_when: the quota that matters counts something other than calls, or the call volume is high
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A usage plan counts requests, not the SMS each request causes, so the per-team SMS budget would still need the service's counters, and at $3.50 per million for the first tranche the 1.5 billion calls a month cost about $4,220.

blocks.text: The bottleneck is the provider, not the service: each provider has its own rate limits and its own bad days. The adapter keeps a circuit breaker per provider; when the primary's error rate crosses a threshold the breaker opens and traffic shifts to the secondary within the 60 s failover target, with the breaker probing the primary in a half-open state. Adapter workers scale on queue age (oldest message age), not on queue length, because age is the SLI the targets are written in.

blocks.caption: The backlog rules this design takes from the Builders' Library article on queue backlogs.
rows: Separate workloads so one backlog cannot starve another
one queue per channel: an SMS backlog never delays push
Keep one tenant from filling everyone's queue
per-team quotas at the API, and a sidelined queue for a team whose messages keep failing
Drain by age, so fresh urgent work is not stuck behind stale work
the transactional class has its own queue per channel; old informational messages past their expiry are dropped rather than sent late
queue age per channel is the alarm, with the threshold at the channel's target

blocks.text: Preferences are read on every send: 5,800 reads per second at peak against a 20-million-row table is a cache job, cache-aside with a short TTL and invalidation on preference change. Per-user rate limits are token buckets keyed by user and channel in the same cache.

blocks.title: Quiet hours: hold, collapse, release
items: A notification that lands inside the user's quiet hours is stored with a release time and the state held; its expiry is still enforced.
The held set per user is capped (assumption: a handful per channel); when the cap is exceeded the newest wins and the older ones are collapsed, so a user does not wake up to 40 pings.
A scheduler re-enqueues held notifications when the window ends; anything past its expiry is dropped and the status store says so.
Transactional notifications (security codes, receipts) skip the hold entirely; that is what the priority class is for.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: who chooses channels, what duplicate means, quiet hours, priority classes, status retention, where personal data lives. Say the numbers aloud: 5,800 notifications per second at peak (4,060 push), a 244,000-message push backlog after a 60 s provider stall, about 400 concurrent provider calls in flight.

0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Notification with its idempotency key of (event, user, channel), Preference, DeviceToken and Address inside the adapter boundary, DeliveryStatus, Template; the send and status endpoints.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: API, preference lookup, a queue per channel and priority class, adapters with breakers and secondary providers, status store, dead letter. Say why the queues are separate.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: duplicates and retries (idempotency key, consumer redelivery, collapse identifiers, bounded retries then failover then dead letter), then backlogs and failover (breakers, scaling on age, per-team quotas and sidelining, quiet-hour holds and collapsing).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x platform (quotas, priority shedding, compliance, regions), and the L3 sentence: the product decision hiding in this design is what to do when the preference service is down, and it should be written down before the review.

Context and scope: Five product teams send push, email and SMS from their own code paths with three providers and no shared dedupe; the incidents of the last quarters (duplicate sends after retries, a provider outage with no failover, no quiet hours). Scope: one internal service for all teams; marketing campaigns and an in-app inbox out of scope.

Goals and non-goals: At-least-once delivery with dedupe so the user sees one message per event; failover within 60 s; preferences and quiet hours; status queryable by the sending team. Non-goals: exactly-once across providers, real-time analytics.
Design: This answer fills it: the API with idempotency keys, the preference lookup, one queue per channel and priority, adapters behind breakers, the status store, the dead-letter view.

Alternatives considered: A library per team (no shared dedupe, three deployments of every provider change); one queue for all channels (SMS backlog delays push); a managed product alone (preferences still need our data), kept as a provider.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security: internal API, per-team credentials, personal data only inside the adapter boundary and the status store, encrypted at rest. Observability: queue age per channel, send success by provider, dedupe hit ratio, breaker state; alert on queue age over the channel target. Cost: per-channel unit cost with SMS the driver, budget with the sending team via a quota. Rollout: shadow mode, then one team's push, then all channels; rollback is a config flag per team.

Review questions the doc must answer: What happens to a notification when the preference service is down (stale cache first, then send push, hold SMS and email); how retries are bounded per provider (3 attempts with jitter, then failover, then dead letter); the dedupe key's lifetime (24 h) and the duplicate it does not catch.
